newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: World leaders celebrate anniversary in Bangladesh.
newsitem.headline: World leaders celebrate anniversary in Bangladesh.

text.p: World leaders attending Bangladesh's 26th independence anniversary on Wednesday paid tribute to the country's founder, Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, saying he was revered by all people who struggled for freedom.
"There has been a bond of solidarity between our two nations," said President Nelson Mandela of South Africa.
"I also remember your support for our struggle," said Yasser Arafat, President of the Palestinian Authority.
Turkish President Suleyman Demirel said: "Turkey and Bangladesh shall move in solidarity and hand in hand."
Mujib, father of Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, was killed with his wife and three sons in the country's first army coup in August, 1975.
Bangladesh proclaimed independence from Pakistan on March 26, 1971, and was liberated on December 16 after a nine-month war in which it received help from India.
Hasina, who came to power following a general election last June, said her government was striving to achieve seven percent economic growth, remove poverty and eradicate illiteracy.
"We will build a happy and prosperous Bangladesh, and make it free from hunger and poverty," she said at the day's main function at Dhaka's historic Suhrawardy garden.
An estimated 200,000 people turned out to listen to Hasina and the visiting leaders.

At the Suhrawardy garden, where Mujib first called for resistance against the Pakistani army on March 7, 1971, Hasina on Wednesday formally lit the "eternal flame" and received the "independence torch" which has travelled across the country over the past 20 days.
Earlier on Wednesday, the visiting leaders laid wreaths at a mausoleum outside Dhaka for those who died in the 1971 war.
The armed forces' bugles played the Last Post at one minute past midnight to commemorate what is officially described as the "black night" genocide on March 25, 1971.
On that night, the Pakistani army gunned down tens of thousands of people in Dhaka -- the capital of what was then East Pakistan -- trying to thwart the independence movement.
